clinicalPearls: Rare disorder of invasive, dense mediastinal fibrosis that encases and compresses vital structures.
In endemic regions the commonest antecedent is prior Histoplasma capsulatum infection; tuberculosis is another recognised trigger.
The fibrosis represents an exuberant immune and fibrotic reaction rather than ongoing active infection.
A diffuse infiltrative form is frequently non-infectious and may belong to the IgG4-related disease spectrum.
Superior vena cava syndrome is a classic presentation; airway, pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein and oesophageal compression also occur.
Two patterns are described: a focal, often calcified granulomatous type and a diffuse infiltrative type.
Pulmonary vein or artery stenosis can cause pulmonary hypertension and mimic chronic thromboembolic disease on perfusion imaging.
Established, burnt-out fibrosis responds poorly to medical therapy; symptomatic vascular or airway stenosis may be palliated with endovascular or airway stenting.
reference.pathophysiology: Fibrosing mediastinitis is characterised by the proliferation of dense, invasive, largely acellular collagenous tissue within the mediastinum that infiltrates and encases vital structures. In endemic regions the commonest antecedent is Histoplasma capsulatum infection, and the disorder is thought to represent an exuberant, immunologically mediated fibrotic response to fungal antigens released from mediastinal lymph nodes rather than ongoing active infection; tuberculosis can provoke a similar reaction. A separate, diffuse infiltrative form is frequently non-infectious and increasingly recognised as part of the IgG4-related disease spectrum, with lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis, while other associations include sarcoidosis, prior radiotherapy and certain drugs; a proportion remain idiopathic. Progressive fibrosis narrows or occludes the superior vena cava, pulmonary arteries and veins, central airways and oesophagus, producing the compressive syndromes that dominate the clinical picture, and pulmonary vascular obstruction may culminate in pulmonary hypertension and right heart strain.
additionalDifferentials: IgG4-related disease with retroperitoneal fibrosis overlap
Superior vena cava thrombosis from indwelling devices
Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (when pulmonary arteries are involved)
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest (infiltrative soft-tissue mass, calcification, vessel and airway encasement)
MRI for soft-tissue characterisation and vascular involvement
Testing for Histoplasma and tuberculosis (serology, antigen assays, interferon-gamma release assay)
Serum IgG4 with tissue IgG4 immunostaining
Biopsy to exclude malignancy and characterise the fibrosis
Echocardiography and, where indicated, right heart catheterisation for pulmonary hypertension
Ventilation-perfusion scanning, which may show perfusion defects mimicking chronic thromboembolic disease
redFlags: Superior vena cava syndrome with facial and upper limb swelling and distended neck veins
Exertional syncope or other signs of pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure
Rapidly progressive dysphagia or central airway compromise
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the extent and bilaterality of vital-structure involvement. Unilateral disease is often compatible with prolonged survival, whereas bilateral central vascular and airway encasement carries substantial morbidity and mortality.
pitfalls: Mistaking the infiltrative mass for malignancy on imaging, or vice versa, without tissue confirmation.
Overlooking treatable IgG4-related disease that may respond to corticosteroids or immunosuppression.
Misattributing perfusion defects to chronic thromboembolic disease and pursuing inappropriate pulmonary endarterectomy.
Expecting antifungal therapy to reverse established, burnt-out fibrosis.
references: Mediastinal disease and thoracic imaging references
management: For the IgG4-related or idiopathic infiltrative form, immunosuppression with corticosteroids and steroid-sparing agents such as rituximab
In histoplasma-associated disease, a trial of azole antifungal therapy such as itraconazole is sometimes used, though established fibrosis often responds poorly
Endovascular relief of vital-structure compression by stenting of the superior vena cava, pulmonary veins or arteries, or central airways for symptomatic obstruction
Symptomatic and supportive care of superior vena cava syndrome, breathlessness and post-obstructive complications
Surveillance for and management of pulmonary hypertension, guided by echocardiography and right-heart catheterisation
Multidisciplinary involvement of respiratory medicine, interventional radiology, thoracic surgery and infectious diseases, with biopsy to exclude malignancy
Escalation for life-threatening central airway or vascular compromise, recognising that extensive open surgical resection is hazardous
